name: Dark Rose
lede: Dark Rose darkens [[rose]], named for the flower, and in our archive it is almost entirely a color of the 1900s, where it runs at nearly ten times the overall rate.

sections.title: A darkened rose
sections.body:
Dark Rose applies our modifier grammar's dark to [[rose]], whose name comes directly from the flower and has named a color in English since the medieval period, long before any formal color dictionary existed [1]. The parent entry used here was crowdsourced in the 2010 xkcd color survey, part of the same large online exercise that supplied [[dark-sienna]] and [[corinthian-purple]] [1].

Its closest measured match is [[pomegranate-purple]], just 2.7 units away and almost the same color; [[popstar]] is nearly as close, [[pomegranate-purple]] a little more distant, and [[pomegranate-purple]] duller still at 3.9 units [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color is rare in our archive overall, matched in only 10 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.04 per cent, as photographed [3]. Seven of those ten are from the 1900s, where the rate runs at about 9.9 times the archive's average, and none at all are dated before 1800 [3]. Kalighat paintings carry it at nearly 25 times the archive rate, though on a single painting out of 96, so the sample is thin [3]. The earliest dated match, from around 1800, shows it covering a little over 11 per cent of its canvas, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].

questions.q: Dark Rose is built by darkening which color?
True or false: Dark Rose is far more common in our archive's 1900s paintings than in earlier centuries.

openers: Rare everywhere in the archive except the 1900s, where it runs ten times as common.
